answers.text: Say the load moves to Friday and two pallets get added. I'd write it as: always output exactly three lines, same order — delivery date, item and quantity, what changed from the original order, nothing else. That keeps the same email coming out as the same three lines every time.

For a week's claims I'd fix the fields and order — date, amount, category, submitter — then total the amount column with nothing hand-adjusted. Duplicate-looking lines (same date, amount, person) get listed separately and flagged, not merged. Two people running this on the same claims should land on the same structure and total.

The price maths is fine — 100 at €48.50 is €4,850. The problem's the dates: the call was the 14th, delivery's meant to be the 19th, but the email calls that 'three days out from today', which doesn't fit. Something in the dates doesn't add up.
62 versus 54 checks out, about 15% up. But 3 late out of 62 isn't 97% — closer to 95%, so the on-time figure's wrong. I didn't spot anything wrong with the stock split, 170 and 170 does make 340.

I'd sign off Output 2 — it shows the two source numbers and the working behind 4.1%. Output 1 just gives the percentage; if it's wrong there's no way to tell from the sentence, you'd have to re-run the query yourself.

I'd send Reply 2, it has the order and credit references so someone can check them later. Reply 1 isn't necessarily wrong, but the '10% credit' can't be checked against anything as written. I wouldn't scrap it though — I'd just add the references first.

1. Address — no, personal, keep it out. 2. Total sales figure, aggregate — yes, fine. 3. Pricing plan — no, not released yet, stays internal. 4. Spec sheet — yes, already public, nothing new exposed. 5. Mobile number — no, personal too.

Pricing and discounts I wouldn't paste in, that's commercially sensitive until the tool's vetted. The confidentiality clause needs care too, it names both companies directly. The delivery schedule's fine as is, nothing sensitive there. Registration details I'd leave out for now as well.

Before it goes to my manager, I cross-check the delivery count and on-time figure against the warehouse log myself, recalculating rather than trusting the draft. I do it every week, right after the draft's done and before it's sent up.

Step 1 matters — a misread order email puts everything after on the wrong track. But the gate needs to sit at step 4, before the confirmation goes out automatically, since once it's sent the customer has a promise in writing. The gate should check extracted items and quantities against the original email, and that stock used is above a safe margin.
